STOP THE GRAB: HANDS OFF AFRICAN RESOURCES CORPORATION 

By: A Concerned Citizen
Juba | 22nd August 2026

South Sudan is watching a dangerous movie we have seen before. And we must say it loudly now before the credits roll: Stop the grabbing of ARC properties.

This week, a letter dated 21st August 2026  from the Ministry of Justice’s Investigation and Prosecution Committee gave African Resources Corporation (ARC)72 hours to surrender a full list of all its vehicles and properties. The letter cites Criminal Case No. 710/2026 and laws on anti-money laundering and criminal procedure.

On the surface, it looks like “law.” But context matters.

The owner of ARC, Former Vice President Benjamin Bol Mel, is currently under house arrest. He has not been convicted of any crime. He has not had his day in court. Yet institutions of the state are already moving to inventory, and effectively take control of the assets of his private company.

That is not justice. That is confiscation before trial.

1. You Cannot Punish a Man Before the c9ourt does
House arrest is a restriction of movement, not a conviction. 
The presumption of innocence is in our Transitional Constitution. It is also in the same Penal Code Act of 2008 that the Committee quoted in its letter.

If the state suspects a crime, investigate. Prosecute. Prove it in court. 
But you do not get to raid a company, seize its asset register, and paralyze its operations while the owner is locked in his home and cannot defend himself.

That is not due process. That is political targeting wearing legal clothes.

2. ARC is Not Government Property
African Resources Corporation is a private company. It employs South Sudanese. It pays taxes. It runs projects. 
Whether you like Benjamin Bol Mel or not, the company has workers, creditors, partners, and contracts that have nothing to do with Case 710/2026.

When you freeze or “request” all assets of a company this way, you don’t just target one man. You target hundreds of families who depend on ARC for salaries. You target suppliers in Konyo Konyo. You target the credibility of private investment in South Sudan.

Who will bring money into this country if companies can be dismantled by committee letter the moment their owner falls out of favor?

3. The Timing Stinks
Let’s call it what it is. 
The moment a senior leader is placed under house arrest, the machinery moves to go after his business. We saw it before. We are seeing it again. 

Using the Anti-Money Laundering Act and Criminal Procedure Act to demand asset lists within 72 hours is legal on paper. But using it selectively, without a conviction, is abuse.
If there is real evidence of crime, take it to court. Get a court order for seizure. Let lawyers argue. Let a judge decide.

“Committees” should not become courts.

4. This Hurts President Kiir and the Country
Mr. Juma Chirilo and others say they “support President Kiir.” The best way to support him is to protect the rule of law around him.

When the state is seen grabbing private property without trial, the President gets the blame. Investors get scared. Citizens lose faith. And our enemies get talking points: “South Sudan is not safe for business.”

Is that what we want?

Our Demands

1.  Stop the asset grab immediately. No seizure, no takeover, no interference with ARC operations until there is a court conviction.
2.  Take it to court.If there is a case, prosecute Benjamin Bol Mel fairly and publicly. Let him defend himself.
3.  Protect ARC workers.The state must guarantee that employees will not lose jobs because of a political case.
4.  Respect the Constitution. Investigation yes. Persecution no.

Final Word

South Sudan has buried too many people. We have also buried too many companies, too many jobs, and too much trust because we confuse politics with justice.

Former VP Benjamin Bol Mel deserves his day in court — not a midnight inventory of his company while he is under house arrest.
ARC deserves to operate under the law — not be dismantled by administrative letters.

If we allow this today, tomorrow it will be your company. Your land. Your car.

Hands off ARC. Let the law take its course. And let the court, not a committee, decide guilt or innocence.

Salary Is a Right, Not a Political Bargaining Chip

Recently, a Member of Parliament from Northern Bahr El Ghazal State made a public statement warning that the people of Aweil, and South Sudan more broadly, will not vote in the upcoming elections unless the government clears their outstanding salaries, which have gone unpaid for two years.

While the demand for unpaid salaries is entirely legitimate, the way it has been framed is problematic and lack civil duty conscience. Tying salary payment to electoral participation or political support reduces a fundamental right to a transactional bargain. This approach is not only politically shallow but also undermines the very principles of citizenship and accountability.

First, salary is an earned right, not a reward for loyalty. Government employees work for their pay. Their salaries are not gifts from the president or any political party. They are legal entitlements backed by employment contracts and public service obligations. No worker should have to chant political slogans or pledge allegiance before receiving what they have already earned. To suggest otherwise is to accept that salaries depend on political favor, which is precisely the kind of system that has enabled the current crisis. It give political elites, who are perpetrators, right over what is not their, I think the MP is not well informed.

Second, elections are a constitutional duty, not a bargaining tool.
Threatening to boycott elections unless salaries are paid confuses two separate issues. Elections belong to the people and the nation; they are not personal property that public employees can offer or withhold in exchange for back pay. Using them as leverage weakens the democratic process and sends the wrong message, that citizens' political participation is for sale, rather than a sovereign right. In elections, all citizens can vote whether they are employed or not.

Third, the real failure is governance, not political support. Two years without salary is a profound failure of state responsibility. Those responsible, whether in executive offices, finance ministries, or oversight bodies, must be held accountable. But accountability requires clear, principled demands. Citizens should say: “Pay us because we worked, and because the law requires it.” Not: “Pay us, and then we will support you.” The former is a demand for justice; the latter is a negotiation that dignifies injustice.

Finally, rights and choices must remain separate. A salary is a right. A vote is a right. Political support is a free choice. None of these should be traded for another. When we mix them, we weaken all three. We give the government an excuse to treat salaries as political favors, and we reduce ourselves to bargaining for what is already ours.

The people of South Sudan deserve their salaries, fully and without delay. But they also deserve a political culture where rights are claimed with dignity, not offered as currency. The cry for justice must be clear, firm, and principled, not conditional, not transactional, and never dependent on a political slogan of Oyee as MP put it.

OPEN LETTER TO H.E. GENERAL SALVA KIIR MAYARDIT

President of the Republic of South Sudan

Subject: URGENT APPEAL FOR THE RELEASE OF DETAINEES HELD IN CONNECTION WITH THE ARC INVESTIGATION

Date: 10th August 2026

Your Excellency,

We, the families and concerned relatives of the remaining detainees at the Blue House, respectfully appeal to Your Excellency to intervene personally and bring an end to their prolonged detention without charge or appearance before a competent court.

We fully support the investigation of any alleged financial wrongdoing involving African Resources Corporation (ARC), crude oil-for-infrastructure arrangements, and public resources. Those responsible for any wrongdoing should account for their actions before the law.

However, an investigation must be based on individual evidence and individual responsibility. No citizen should remain in detention merely because he is associated with a broader investigation.

Your Excellency, some of these detainees have now spent six to nearly nine months in detention without being formally charged or presented before a competent court.

This is deeply concerning.

We also respectfully remind Your Excellency that you directed that the investigation be expedited within 30 days, that persons found not implicated be released, and that those against whom sufficient evidence exists be taken to court.

That 30-day period has now expired, yet some remain in detention.

We therefore respectfully ask: Why should your own directive not be implemented?

If there is evidence against any detainee, let that evidence be presented before a court.

If there is no evidence, let the person go home.

The ARC investigation should follow the evidence

If the investigation concerns crude oil-for-infrastructure funds, accountability should follow the complete contractual and financial chain.

The relevant former officials of the Ministries of Justice, Finance and Planning, Roads and Bridges, Petroleum, the Office of the President, as well as relevant officials of the Bank of South Sudan, contractors and technical officials who authorised, supervised, certified or paid for the relevant contracts should be examined where appropriate.

ARC itself should account for:

the contracts it received; the resources or payments it received; the work it performed; and how those resources were utilised.

The proper principle should be simple:

Follow the contract. Follow the money. Follow the work. Follow the evidence.

That is how a credible investigation should be conducted.

The investigation must not become indefinite detention

We are also deeply concerned by allegations concerning the reported US$3.5 million investigation fee and claims of a possible financial interest in funds recovered.

If these allegations are accurate, they deserve independent scrutiny.

An investigation into public corruption must be conducted solely in the public interest. Investigators should have no financial incentive to secure particular outcomes.

Your Excellency, the families are not asking that anyone who committed an offence be protected.

We are asking for equal application of the law.

Those against whom there is evidence should face court.

Those against whom there is no evidence should be released.

Your Excellency, South Sudan needs peace

As the country approaches the December 2026 general elections, South Sudan needs reconciliation, confidence, and political stability.

The continued detention of former government officials without charge is creating deep anxiety among their families, communities, and political constituencies.

Keeping people in detention without trial does not strengthen the state; it weakens confidence in the state.

Your Excellency, releasing individuals against whom no evidence exists, would not mean abandoning the fight against corruption.

It would demonstrate that South Sudan can distinguish between investigation and punishment, accusation and evidence, and political disagreement and criminal responsibility.

We therefore humbly appeal to Your Excellency to:

Immediately review the cases of all remaining detainees;

Release those against whom the investigation has established no evidence; and

Direct that anyone against whom credible evidence exists be formally charged and brought before a competent court without further delay.

The remaining detainees are:

1. Hon. Dr. Marial Dongrin Ater
2. Amb. Ajing Deng Ajing
3. Maj. Gen. (PSC) Dominic Juk Chom
4. Hon.Eng. Deng Lual Wol
5. Hon. Simon Akuei Deng
6. Hon. Eng. John Khot Chol
7. Hon. Moses Makur Deng
8. Dr. Chan Andrea Chan
9. Mr. Majok Thiel Koch
10. Mr. Bol Malang Ngong

Your Excellency,

The families are not asking for special treatment.

They are asking for the law to be applied.

They are asking that detention does not become a substitute for trial and that an investigation does not become an indefinite punishment.

Release those who have been cleared.
Charge those against whom there is evidence.
Take the cases to court.
Let justice not detention determine guilt.

At this important moment in our nation’s history, justice can become the bridge to peace.

Respectfully,

Representatives of the Families of the Detainees.

The Core Revenue Collection Contradiction: Who Pays, Who Is Exempt?

In July 2026, Gen. Pieng Deng Kuol was appointed to chair a High-Level Committee on Economic Reform mandated, among other things, to strengthen and reform national revenue collection. On 27 July 2026, the Committee met in Nimule, Eastern Equatoria State, with representatives of clearing agencies, commercial banks, customs authorities and security institutions. During the meeting, the Chairperson reportedly emphasised that increasing government revenue was a national priority and called for greater coordination among institutions responsible for revenue collection. He further directed that suppliers, contractors and subcontractors comply with their tax obligations before their goods are cleared.

The objective of improving domestic revenue mobilisation is neither controversial nor unreasonable. A state cannot provide security, pay its civil servants, maintain public institutions or finance development without a functioning and equitable fiscal system. The problem, however, arises when the government demands strict compliance from some taxpayers while leaving unresolved questions about the fiscal treatment of other territories administered or financed by the same state.

This raises a fundamental question that the Ministry of Finance and Planning, the South Sudan National Revenue Authority (NRA) and the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform should answer publicly:

Does Abyei form part of South Sudan’s national fiscal and revenue-collection system, and if so, why is its treatment apparently different from that imposed on taxpayers at places such as Nimule?

Since the establishment of the Abyei Special Administrative Area by the Government of South Sudan in July 2015, questions have repeatedly arisen concerning the collection, administration and remittance of non-oil revenues generated in or through Abyei. If revenues generated within an area administered and supported by the Government of South Sudan are outside the oversight of the national revenue system, the government owes the public a clear legal and fiscal explanation.

This is not merely a political question. It is a question of fiscal equality, institutional accountability and the rule of law.

A trader operating at Nimule is expected to comply with customs requirements, taxation and other government charges before goods can enter the country. Contractors and suppliers are instructed to meet their tax obligations before their transactions can proceed. Yet if another area benefiting from the political, administrative or financial support of the Republic of South Sudan is permitted to operate outside the same national revenue architecture, taxpayers are entitled to ask why.

The concern becomes even more serious when the person responsible for leading a national economic-reform initiative is politically and administratively associated with an area whose fiscal relationship with the national government remains unclear.

Gen. Pieng Deng Kuol’s appointment therefore creates an obvious perception of a conflict of interest, irrespective of his personal intentions. A national revenue-reform committee must be seen to apply one standard across the country. Its credibility depends not only on what it demands from taxpayers but also on whether its leadership is prepared to subject every territory, institution and political constituency to the same fiscal rules.

The issue should therefore not be reduced to an accusation against the Ngok Dinka community or the people of Abyei. Ordinary citizens in Abyei should not be blamed for decisions made by political and administrative authorities. The real issue is the governance of public revenue and whether national fiscal institutions have equal authority throughout territories administered, funded or claimed by the Republic of South Sudan.

If Abyei has a special legal or constitutional fiscal status that exempts it from the ordinary national revenue framework, the Government of South Sudan should publish the legal instrument establishing that exemption and explain precisely what revenues are excluded, why they are excluded and who has authority to collect them.

If no such exemption exists, then the NRA should have a clear mandate to exercise appropriate revenue oversight in Abyei in accordance with South Sudanese law.

Anything less creates a two-tier fiscal system: one in which ordinary traders, businesses, contractors and civil servants are expected to finance the state while certain politically sensitive areas remain outside effective national revenue oversight.

That is precisely the kind of contradiction that can destroy public confidence in economic reform.

There is also a broader fiscal question that cannot be ignored. If the Government of South Sudan continues to allocate public funds to support the administration and operations of the Abyei Special Administrative Area, while revenues generated there are not transparently incorporated into the national fiscal framework, the public deserves to know the financial rationale.

How much does the national government allocate to the Abyei Administration each financial year? What revenues are collected within the area? Which institution collects them? Where are those revenues deposited? Are they reported to the national Treasury? And what legal framework governs their collection and expenditure?

These are basic questions of public financial management, not questions of ethnicity.

The same principle must apply to the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform itself. Economic reform cannot mean increasing the tax burden on already struggling businesses while leaving politically protected revenue streams outside the national system. Nor can reform succeed if national institutions are perceived as instruments for extracting resources from some communities while protecting others from the same obligations.

The Government therefore needs to resolve this contradiction openly.

First, the Ministry of Finance and Planning should issue a comprehensive public clarification on the fiscal and revenue status of the Abyei Special Administrative Area.

Second, the National Revenue Authority should clarify whether it has legal jurisdiction to administer and audit non-oil revenue collected in Abyei and, if not, identify the legal basis for that limitation.

Third, the Government should publish the annual budgetary allocations made to the Abyei Administration and provide an account of how those funds are financed.

Fourth, the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform should disclose whether Abyei falls within the scope of its revenue-reform mandate and, if it does, explain what measures are being taken to bring revenue collection there into the national fiscal framework.

Finally, Gen. Pieng Deng should address the perceived conflict of interest created by his position. If the fiscal arrangements governing Abyei place him in a position where he cannot objectively advocate for the same revenue standards nationwide, he should consider recusing himself from matters directly concerning Abyei—or, where the conflict is substantive and unavoidable, stepping aside from the committee’s leadership.

South Sudan does not need a revenue system based on political privilege. It needs a system based on law, transparency, equality and accountability.

The Government cannot credibly tell citizens at Nimule, Juba, Wau, Malakal or elsewhere that everyone must pay while failing to provide a convincing explanation of whether the same principle applies in Abyei.

Revenue reform must therefore begin with a simple principle:

No taxpayer should be compelled to carry a burden from which politically connected constituencies are exempt.

If the Government genuinely intends to reform South Sudan’s economy, it must first eliminate the perception that there are two fiscal systems—one for ordinary taxpayers and another for politically protected territories.

Until that contradiction is resolved, the public has every reason to question whether the current revenue-reform programme represents genuine institutional reform or merely another mechanism for extracting more resources from citizens without establishing equal accountability at the centre.

A Crisis of Institutional Protocol in the Eyes of Influential Leader Adut Salva Kiir Mayardit: Police Promotions, Ministerial Authority, and the Rule of Law in South Sudan

Recent developments within the South Sudan National Police Service have raised serious questions about institutional discipline, administrative procedures, and the relationship between the leadership of the Ministry of Interior and the Inspector General of Police.

There are growing concerns that the Inspector General of Police, Gen. Saed Chawul Lom, has once again taken unilateral decisions regarding promotions within the police service. This is the second occasion on which large-scale, or what some observers consider "inflated," promotions have been announced without sufficient regard for the established administrative procedures and protocols expected to govern promotions within a professional security institution.

The central concern is not merely the number of officers promoted, but the process through which such promotions are made. In any disciplined institution, particularly a national police service, promotions are expected to follow clear criteria, including professional qualifications, training, experience, performance, seniority where applicable, and the recommendations and approvals required by the relevant authorities. When such procedures are bypassed, the credibility of the entire promotion system is called into question.

Of particular concern are cases in which some individuals who have received police ranks have not undergone the necessary police training or orientation expected of members of the police service. Such a practice raises fundamental questions about professionalism, competence, and the institutional identity of the police service. A police rank should represent more than a title; it should signify training, responsibility, discipline, experience, and readiness to perform the duties entrusted to an officer by the Republic.

The concern, therefore, extends beyond individual promotions. It touches on the broader question of whether South Sudan is building professional institutions governed by rules or institutions increasingly influenced by individual discretion.

The Importance of Ministry of Interior Protocols

The Ministry of Interior occupies a critical position within the national security architecture of South Sudan. The police service does not operate in isolation from the ministry responsible for its political and administrative oversight. Consequently, institutional decisions affecting the structure, ranks, and administration of the police should be handled through established channels.

The repeated promotions undertaken outside the expected ministerial protocols deserve serious public and institutional scrutiny.

This should not be interpreted as opposition to the promotion of deserving police officers. On the contrary, deserving officers should be promoted, recognized, and rewarded. However, promotions become problematic when questions arise regarding whether the correct procedures were followed, whether the appropriate authorities were consulted, and whether those receiving ranks possess the qualifications and professional background required for the positions they occupy.

A professional police service cannot be built on shortcuts.

Questions Concerning the Relationship Between the Minister and the IGP

Another matter that has attracted public attention is the relationship between the Inspector General of Police and the incumbent Minister of Interior, Hon. Lt. Gen. Aleu Ayieny Aleu.

There are growing concerns that the authority of the Minister has, on several occasions, been undermined by actions attributed to the Inspector General. This raises a much larger institutional question: Who ultimately provides political and administrative oversight of the national police service?

The Minister of Interior is the political head of the ministry, while the Inspector General is responsible for the professional command and administration of the police service. These roles are distinct, but they must operate within a framework of cooperation, accountability, and respect for the chain of command established by law and government policy.

A subordinate officer should not be perceived as competing with, humiliating, or overriding the authority of the political head of the institution. Likewise, ministerial authority should not be exercised in a manner that interferes with the professional responsibilities legally assigned to the police command.

The solution, therefore, is not personal confrontation but institutional clarity.

The Question of Insubordination

The strongest criticism emerging from this controversy concerns institutional insubordination.

When the Inspector General makes major decisions affecting police ranks and structures without appropriate consultation with the responsible ministry, and such conduct is repeated despite previous concerns, the matter should be examined through the appropriate governmental and legal mechanisms.

South Sudan cannot afford a situation in which senior officials interpret their positions according to personal power rather than institutional responsibility.

The history of the liberation struggle has produced leaders who sacrificed enormously for the establishment of the Republic. Gen. Aleu Ayieny Aleu, like many members of the liberation generation, has a political and historical background that commands respect. His appointment as Minister of Interior should therefore be understood within the broader framework of strengthening national institutions and advancing reforms in the security sector.

However, the legitimacy of any minister's authority must ultimately derive from the Constitution, the laws, and the structures of government—not merely from liberation credentials.

Similarly, the authority of the Inspector General must come from the law and the office he occupies, not from personal influence or political alliances.

Political Protection

There are growing concerns that certain senior figures believe they possess sufficient political influence to shield themselves from accountability within the Ministry of Interior.

The existence of such perceptions is itself troubling.

No public official should operate under the assumption that political connections make him untouchable. Neither the Minister of Interior, nor the Inspector General of Police, nor any other government official should be above institutional accountability.

South Sudan's institutions will become stronger only when public office is understood as a responsibility rather than personal authority.

Reform Requires Institutional Discipline

The reported controversy is particularly significant because the Ministry of Interior requires meaningful reform. The country needs a police service that is professional, politically neutral in its operational duties, properly trained, adequately equipped, and accountable to the law.

Reform cannot succeed if institutional procedures are repeatedly ignored.

If promotions are necessary, let them be conducted transparently. Let the relevant committees examine the qualifications of candidates. Let training requirements be respected. Let the appropriate ministry authorities participate in accordance with the law. Let deserving officers receive recognition based on merit, competence, experience, and service.

That would strengthen the police institution rather than weaken it.

The country should not create a situation in which police ranks become instruments of political patronage or personal loyalty. A rank in the National Police Service must carry professional meaning and public confidence.

A Call for Institutional Review

In light of these concerns, there is a legitimate basis for calling for an institutional review of the recent promotion decisions.

Such a review should establish:

- Whether the promotions complied with applicable laws, regulations, and Ministry of Interior procedures;
- Whether the individuals promoted possessed the necessary qualifications and police training;
- Whether the appropriate ministerial and police authorities participated in the promotion process;
- Whether previous promotion decisions followed the same procedures;
- Whether there were administrative disagreements between the Ministry of Interior and the police leadership;
- Whether any individual exercised authority beyond the powers legally assigned to his office; and
- What measures should be taken to prevent similar institutional disputes in the future.

This would not amount to undermining the police. Rather, it would strengthen the police service by ensuring that its leadership operates within a predictable and accountable institutional framework.

The Republic Must Come Before Individuals

The fundamental issue is bigger than Gen. Saed Chawul Lom, Hon. Aleu Ayieny Aleu, Gen. Kon John Akot, or any other individual mentioned in the controversy.

South Sudan must move away from a culture in which institutions are perceived through the personalities occupying them.

Ministers come and go. Inspectors General come and go. Generals come and go. Political leaders come and go. But the institutions of the Republic must remain.

If the Inspector General has acted within his lawful authority, that authority should be demonstrated through the applicable legal and administrative provisions. If he has exceeded his mandate, the appropriate authorities should address the matter through lawful institutional mechanisms.

Likewise, if the Minister of Interior has acted within his mandate, his authority should be respected. If there are disagreements between the Minister and the Inspector General, those disagreements should be resolved through government procedures rather than public confrontation, political speculation, or competing demonstrations of power.

Conclusion

The second round of controversial police promotions should not be reduced to a personal disagreement between senior government officials. It presents an opportunity for South Sudan to ask a more fundamental question: Are our security institutions governed by established rules, or are they increasingly shaped by individual discretion and political influence?

The people of South Sudan deserve a police service that commands respect because of its professionalism, not because of the rank of the individuals leading it.

Where promotion procedures have been bypassed, the matter should be investigated. Where individuals without the required professional training have been granted police ranks, the matter should be reviewed. Where ministerial authority has been disregarded, the relevant constitutional and administrative mechanisms should clarify the boundaries of authority. Where any official has exceeded his mandate, accountability should follow regardless of political connections or personal influence.

The Minister of Interior should be able to pursue his reform agenda without being undermined by subordinates, while the Inspector General should be able to perform his professional responsibilities without undue political interference. The two offices should complement one another—not compete for institutional supremacy.

Ultimately, no individual should be bigger than the institution, and no institution should be bigger than the law.

South Sudan needs disciplined leadership, professional security institutions, transparent promotion procedures, and respect for the chain of command. The country has paid too high a price to allow personal rivalries, perceived political protection, or administrative shortcuts to weaken the institutions for which generations of South Sudanese struggled.

“YOUR PEOPLE ARE HOLDING THE COWS’ HORNS WHILE OTHERS ARE MILKING THE COWS”

What struck me most was the way Parieng described the situation facing the Bul community.

He told me:

“Your people who stood firmly with President Salva Kiir are now holding the cows’ horns, while the sons of Bahr el Ghazal are milking the cows.”

The statement was painful, but it was intended to describe what he considers a serious imbalance between sacrifice and reward.

According to him, while the sons and daughters of the Bul community have remained heavily engaged in the restoration of law and order and have continued to defend the government and the country's oil infrastructure, they have not received proportional opportunities within the very oil industry they have helped protect.

A HISTORY OF SACRIFICE

His argument goes beyond the current employment controversy.

He reminded me that the oilfields in Greater Unity have historically depended on the security provided by local communities. He argued that South Sudan's oil reserves, including the oil-producing areas around Mayom and Kaikang in Blocks 4S and 4N, have faced security challenges throughout their history.

During the Sudan period, he said, many people were aware of the relationship between the armed forces associated with President Omar al-Bashir and the forces associated with Paulino Matip. According to his interpretation, that relationship contributed to the security arrangements that made continued oil operations possible in the region.

His point was simple: without the contribution and sacrifice of local sons and daughters, oil production in these areas would have faced enormous difficulties.

The same argument, he said, applies to the period following South Sudan's independence.

THE SACRIFICE OF 2013

He particularly referred to the outbreak of war in 2013, when members of the Bul community chose to defend the government despite facing criticism from sections of the Nuer community.

He recalled how some people were even called “Nuer-wew” because of their decision to stand with the government.

Yet, according to him, the community continued to fight without expecting immediate rewards, while its sons and daughters were deployed to various frontlines to protect the government and maintain security.

From 2013 to the present, he argued, the community has continued to make sacrifices.

His central question, therefore, was:

If the community has consistently provided the security that enables the oil industry to operate, why should its sons and daughters remain excluded from meaningful employment opportunities within that same industry?

MY HEARTFELT RESPONSE TO HIM

I listened to Parieng carefully. His argument was emotional, but it also raised questions that deserve serious consideration.

Communities that contribute to the security and stability of oil-producing areas should not have to beg for recognition. At the same time, employment in the oil sector should be based on qualifications, competence, experience and transparent recruitment processes, regardless of a person's community of origin.

If there are genuine cases of nepotism or unqualified appointments, they should be investigated transparently. If the recruitment process is fair, the institutions responsible should be able to demonstrate that fairness through clear criteria and transparent records.

Ultimately, the issue should not be about replacing one form of domination with another. It should be about ensuring that all South Sudanese citizens, including the communities surrounding the oilfields, have a fair opportunity to participate in the country's economic development.

Successful people always have two things on their lips: silence and a smile. Smile to solve problems, and silence to avoid problems. Master both, and nothing can easily disturb your peace.

TITLE: SOUTH SUDAN’S “COOL WAR”: WHEN PEACE BECOMES MORE DANGEROUS THAN BULLETS.

June,12/2026

By Simon Yai Deng | Student of International Relations & Diplomacy, Diploma holder in Accounting & Finance.

SUBHEAD: We survived the hot war of guns. But are we losing the cool war of systems?

We were taught as children that war is loud. War is gunfire at night. War is running from your home with only your life.

We survived that war. We signed peace. We raised flag🇸🇸🕊️. We said “Never Again.”

But since from 2013 to present , many South Sudanese are asking a painful question: Did the war really end, or did it just change uniforms?

As a student of International Relations and Diplomacy, I have learned there are two types of war:

1. HOT WAR: The War We All See
Hot war is bullets, tanks, and displacement. It is CNN, UN reports, and refugee camps. It is dangerous, yes. But it is honest. In hot war, the enemy wears a uniform. In hot war, citizens unite. In hot war, the world sends aid and says “We see you.”

2. COOL WAR: The War We Don’t Name
Cool war is silence. It is hardship designed into systems. No bombs drop, but dreams die daily.
Cool war is:
>Salary delays for a quiet times while inflation eats what’s left. That’s not “economic delay”. That’s economic violence. It makes a teacher, nurse, or soldier powerless in his own country.
>Hospitals without medicine, schools without education (qualify teachers). When the state cannot heal the sick or teach the child, it sends one message: “Citizen, you are on your own.” People don’t become “nothing” overnight. They are made to feel like nothing, slowly.
>Youth with degrees but no dignity.  We graduate with Diplomas, Bachelor’s degrees, Master’s degrees and remain unemployed because in South Sudan many job opportunities depend on who you know, then wait years for a chance. Cool war doesn’t kill the body. It kills ambition. And a nation without ambitious youth is a nation preparing for its next hot war.

THE DANGEROUS BELIEF
People believe hot war is the only dangerous war. So we fear gunfire more than we fear empty clinics. We protest bullets more than we question broken systems.

But IR teaches me: Cool war kills more, because it kills hope first, then people. Hot war makes headlines. Cool war makes orphans of the future. By the time we notice, an entire generation already feels like “nothing” to those in power.

MY CONSTRUCTIVE APPEAL AS A STUDENT, NOT AN ENEMY
I write this not as an opposition voice, but as a son of this soil. My criticism is patriotism, not treason.

To our leaders: Your legacy will not be measured by how well you survived war. It will be measured by how well you built peace. Peace is not just the absence of gunfire. Peace is the presence of salary on time, medicine in hospitals, jobs for graduates, and dignity for every citizen.

Stop the cool war by design. Build systems that make citizens feel like owners, not strangers, in South Sudan. Because a government that makes its youth feel invisible today… will have no youth to defend it tomorrow.

CLOSING TRUTH
In scripture: “You shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free.”
In diplomacy: Truth, told with wisdom, builds nations.

South Sudan does not need more silence. We need more courage — the courage of leaders to fix systems, and the courage of citizens to speak truth without fear.

The hot war took our past. Let us not allow the cool war to steal our future.

The author is a South Sudanese citizen and a forth year student of International Relations & Diplomacy, SIU, Diploma holder in Accounting & Finance, CVI. He writes on governance, youth, and national development.

High-level consultative meetings involving South Sudan opposition groups are underway in Dar El Salaam, Tanzania, as part of efforts to revive an inclusive peace process amid stalled implementation of the 2018 peace agreement.

The consultations are being held under the auspices of former Tanzanian president and African Union envoy on South Sudan, Jakaya Kikwete.

The meetings, which are being conducted separately with each group, began on Thursday and are expected to conclude on Friday.

Participants include:

1. the United People’s Alliance (UPA), led by Pagan Amum.

2. the South Sudan Opposition Movements Alliance (SSOMA), led by Gen. Thomas Cirillo.

3. the country’s second-largest party, SPLM-IO, led by Dr. Riek Machar.

4. the People’s Coalition for Civil Action (PCCA).

5. the Federal Democratic Party, led by Gabriel Changson Chang.

Speaking to Radio African Press on Thursday, UPA Secretary General Lual Dau said the group’s delegation, led by Amum, was taking part in consultations with the AU team.

The UPA high-level delegation includes:

1. Gen. Paul Malong Awan.
2. Gen. Marko Laku.
3. Gen. Stephen Buay Rolnyang.
4. Gen. Oyai Deng Ajak.
5. Dr. Cirino Hiteng and other members,” Lual said.

Lual said the opposition groups had presented their views on the failure to fully implement the revitalised peace agreement, the government’s withdrawal from the Tumaini Peace Initiative, and violations of the peace deal.

“We proposed that the only way forward for an inclusive peace process is to begin with the release of all political detainees in the country and the return of all parties to an inclusive dialogue to draw a clear roadmap for peace,” he said.

He said the consultations were intended to help the AU better understand the political and security situation in South Sudan and gather the opposition’s views on challenges facing the country and possible pathways to peace.

Lual said the talks followed earlier consultations held by Kikwete in Juba, where he met government officials and political parties.

“After these meetings, AU envoy Kikwete will have the full picture on how to address the challenges of South Sudan and how best he can approach issues of peace in South Sudan,” Lual said.

Gai Mayen Luk, a senior SPLM-IO member, said the group had sent two representatives to attend the meetings after what he described as an initial misunderstanding over the invitation was resolved.

“We have sent Hon. Gatluak Gabriel Deng and Hon. Gatluak Michael. They are already in Dar es Salaam for the consultative meetings,” Mayen said.

A PCCA member, who declined to be named, confirmed the group had met Kikwete on Thursday and briefed him on challenges surrounding implementation of previous peace agreements.

The official said the group urged the AU to mobilise regional and international support for an inclusive dialogue process and ensure accountability for violations of peace agreements.

“If the AU does not have a strong voice, peace will not prevail in South Sudan,” he said.

Kikwete visited Juba in early April on a three-day fact-finding mission during which he met President Salva Kiir and political parties based in the capital.

Kikwete, Tanzania’s fourth president from 2005 to 2015, was appointed in March by the African Union chairperson as High Representative for the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, with a special mandate on South Sudan.

The consultations fall under the African Union’s Ad Hoc High-Level Committee on South Sudan, known as the C5, which supports implementation of the 2018 peace agreement and promotes inclusive dialogue ahead of elections.

In February, the C5 called for measures including elections in December 2026, the release of detainees, particularly Machar, inclusive dialogue among parties, and a ceasefire.
